author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Recognize misleading FPS readings in PS2 emulation
summary: Cross-check FPS with emulation speed, VPS, frame time, audio cadence, limiter state, title frame-rate design, and visible motion so duplicated or skipped presentation is not mistaken for correct full-speed gameplay.
heroAlt: PCSX2 window title showing FPS and speed counters that require contextual interpretation

blocks.text: Ask what the counter counts before trusting its value

A title designed for 30 rendered frames per second can still run at correct 100 percent emulation speed, while a display counter may report repeated presentations near 60. Conversely, a high FPS value can coexist with fast-forward, frame duplication, skipped output, slow audio, or unstable pacing. Read emulation speed, video rate, limiter state, and frame time together, then compare them with a known in-game timing event.
Do not tune cycle rate, speed controls, or frame skipping merely to make one FPS number match the display refresh rate. That can change game timing while the counter looks reassuring.

items: A reproducible timer, animation, lap, or scripted sequence in the game.
FPS, emulation speed, VPS, and frame-time counters available together where possible.
Normal limiter, frame skipping disabled, and fast-forward inactive.
Stable renderer, resolution, display refresh, and synchronization settings.
Audio captured as an independent cadence reference.

blocks.text: Triangulate counter, cadence, and game time

items: 1. Cold-boot the title and confirm all speed controls are at normal values.
2. Run the timing event while recording wall-clock and in-game duration.
3. Note FPS, VPS, emulation speed, frame time, and limiter state at the same timestamp.
4. Observe whether displayed motion repeats frames or skips unevenly.
5. Compare audio pitch and synchronization through the complete event.
6. Test one known 30-fps scene and one known 60-field or 60-fps interface when available.
7. Repeat after disabling only a diagnostic overlay if its cost is suspected.
8. Label each metric precisely in the report instead of writing only '60 FPS'.

blocks.text: Correct emulation means the guest progresses at intended time with synchronized audio and acceptable pacing. Rendered frames, video presentations, fields, and host refreshes are related but not interchangeable. A wall-clock event exposes cases where a visually plausible number accompanies slow or accelerated simulation.
The reading is trustworthy when numeric counters, wall-clock timing, visible cadence, and audio tell the same story.

items: Limiter and speed-control state are documented.
The game's intended frame behavior is not confused with host refresh.
Wall-clock and in-game duration agree at normal speed.
Audio remains correctly pitched and synchronized.
Frame-time evidence reveals pacing hidden by an average FPS value.
The overlay shows a rolling average during a short hitch: use interval or frame-time evidence.
Fast-forward remains bound to a pressed control: reset input and repeat.
A 30-fps title is called half speed from FPS alone: verify game time.
Capture changes presentation rate: repeat with matched overhead.

blocks.text: Return limiter, synchronization, and frame skipping to the verified defaults, disable temporary counters that add clutter or overhead, and cold-boot the timing event once. Retain a short legend explaining which metric represented simulation, presentation, and frame time.
PAL and NTSC timing require regional context

Nominal video rates and game conversions differ across regions, and some titles change cadence between menus, gameplay, and FMV. Record the disc serial and region before comparing a counter to another release or online result.
